notes.claim: In a fraction the top number (numerator) counts the parts you have and the bottom number (denominator) says how many equal parts the whole is divided into.
A fraction is a number with its own place on the number line, and the whole it is a fraction of can be a shape, a length, a number or a set of objects.
Fractions that look different can name the same number: they sit at the same point on the number line, and multiplying top and bottom by the same number does not change the value.
Comparing fractions is only valid when both fractions refer to the same whole.
A fraction is a number on the number line: marking off a lengths of 1/b from 0 gives an interval whose endpoint locates the number a/b.
A fraction can be read as the ratio of two whole numbers, and every fraction in a family of equivalent fractions occupies the same single point on the number line.
Fractions that are equivalent are the same number because they are located at the same point on the number line.
An improper fraction written as a whole number with a fraction is called a mixed number, and a mixed number gives a good sense of the overall size of the number.
Improper fractions are used when multiplying and dividing; mixed numbers may be preferred for adding and subtracting.
Introductory pages say a fraction is a part of something and represents more than 0 but less than 1; fuller sources treat fractions as numbers that can exceed 1 (improper fractions, mixed numbers).
notes.contested: BBC Bitesize KS1/KS2 pages define a fraction as a part of a whole between 0 and 1 (a simplification for young children); NRICH, Common Core and BBC KS3 treat fractions as numbers that may be greater than 1.

notes.claim: The whole a fraction refers to can be a shape, a length, a number or a set of objects.
Fractions are always divided into equal parts: the denominator counts how many equal parts there are in total, and the numerator counts how many of them you have.
The denominator indicates how many of the parts make up a unit or a whole.
A whole can be divided into any number of equal parts, and equal parts do not need to look the same shape.
Comparisons of fractions are valid only when the two fractions refer to the same whole.
A common error is to treat the numerator and denominator as two independent whole numbers rather than as one fraction.
Unit fractions can be compared and ordered by looking at the denominator: the greater the denominator, the smaller the fraction.
When fractions have the same numerators, the denominators are compared, and the greater denominator gives the smaller fraction.
A common misconception is to compare fractions by whole-number size, judging 1/5 greater than 1/2 because 5 is greater than 2; researchers call this whole-number bias.
The denominator says how many equal parts the whole is divided into, so a bigger denominator means the whole has been cut into more pieces.

Cutting every slice into 2 gives twice as many slices, and you then need twice as many of them for the same amount; multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number does not change what the fraction represents.
Equivalent fractions are made by multiplying both the numerator and the denominator by the same number.
Equivalent fractions name the same number: they sit at the same point on the number line.
A rational number can be thought of as a whole family of equivalent fractions, all at the same point on the number line.
To compare fractions with unlike denominators, find equivalent fractions for both so that they share the same denominator.
When fractions have the same numerators, the one with the greater denominator is smaller.
Multiplying the top and bottom of each fraction by the denominator of the other gives a common denominator and keeps each fraction's value the same.
Comparisons are valid only when the two fractions refer to the same whole.
Judging fractions by their whole numbers (1/5 greater than 1/2 because 5 is greater than 2) is a documented misconception.
When the denominators are the same, you add the numerators; to subtract, subtract the numerators and the denominator remains the same.
Adding halves to halves is counting halves; adding fractions with different denominators needs one or both fractions changed so that they have the same denominator.
To add or subtract fractions that are not related, the product of the two denominators provides a common denominator.
Converting to equivalent fractions by multiplying top and bottom by the same number keeps the value of each fraction the same.
The word 'of' can be replaced by 'multiplied by': three-quarters times one-half is three-eighths.
To multiply fractions, multiply the numerators for the new numerator and the denominators for the new denominator, then simplify where necessary.
Half of two-fifths is two-tenths, which simplifies to one-fifth: taking a fraction of a fraction gives a smaller piece.
Area models (a rectangle cut both ways) are used to represent the multiplication of two fractions and to see why the rule multiplies numerators and denominators.
Dividing one number by a fraction asks how many times that fraction fits into the number.
3 divided by a quarter can be read as how many quarters there are in 3, which is 12: a small piece gives a big count.
The reciprocal of a fraction swaps numerator and denominator; a number times its reciprocal is 1, and the reciprocal says how many times the fraction fits into 1.
How many of a fraction are in one is one divided by that fraction, so dividing any number by that fraction is that number times the reciprocal.
To divide fractions, multiply the first fraction by the reciprocal of the second, which is easier than dividing by a fraction directly.
